# Streaming pebble-run codec

Implement the library in `starter/` for an in-memory fictional byte compressor.
Keep the public API below compatible; internal types, representation, helpers,
and algorithms are yours to choose. Add your own useful tests. The library must
not read files, contact services, print payloads, or panic on any API input.
Ordinary allocation failure is outside this task's contract. Bytes are opaque;
there is no text normalization, and byte values including zero are valid data.

## Wire format

A stream consists of `(count, value)` byte pairs and a single zero count byte
that ends the stream. Counts 1 through 255 mean that many copies of `value`.
For example, `aaa\0\0b` encodes as `[3, 97, 2, 0, 1, 98, 0]`. An empty stream
is `[0]`. No bytes may follow the end marker, including a second end marker.
A decoder accepts adjacent pairs with the same value; it does not require a
canonical wire encoding. Missing a value or the end marker is truncation.

An encoder produces the canonical encoding: combine equal adjacent input bytes
across calls, split each maximal run into as many 255-byte runs as possible,
then one residual run if needed. Emit each full 255-byte run immediately.
Hold an incomplete run until a different byte arrives or `finish` is called.
Do not insert chunk boundaries into the encoding.

## API

The package and crate name is `pebble_runs`. Expose:

```rust
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum Error { Closed, Truncated, LimitExceeded, TrailingData, Failed }

pub struct Encoder { /* private */ }
impl Encoder {
    pub fn new() -> Self;
    pub fn push(&mut self, input: &[u8]) -> Result<Vec<u8>, Error>;
    pub fn finish(&mut self) -> Result<Vec<u8>, Error>;
}

#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub struct Decoded {
    pub consumed: usize,
    pub bytes: Vec<u8>,
    pub ended: bool,
}
pub struct Decoder { /* private */ }
impl Decoder {
    pub fn new(max_decoded_bytes: usize) -> Self;
    pub fn push(&mut self, input: &[u8], output_limit: usize)
        -> Result<Decoded, Error>;
    pub fn finish(&mut self) -> Result<(), Error>;
}
```

## Encoder behavior

`push` consumes its entire input and returns only the bytes ready at that call.
An empty push before completion returns no bytes. `finish` returns any pending
run followed by the end marker. Repeating `finish` succeeds with an empty
vector, so concatenating all returned vectors produces exactly one stream.
Every `push` after completion, even an empty push, returns `Closed`.

## Decoder behavior

`push` takes a wire prefix and an output budget. `consumed` counts only bytes
consumed from that call's input. The caller must resubmit the unconsumed suffix.
The decoder may retain a count awaiting its value and the remaining repetitions
of one decoded run, but must not retain unconsumed input. It can therefore
produce pending output even when a later call supplies empty input.

For an active decoder and a positive budget, work greedily in stream order:
drain pending repetitions first, then read pairs and emit their repetitions.
Stop immediately when `bytes.len() == output_limit`; do not inspect subsequent
wire bytes even if they are a terminator or error. Otherwise stop only on input
exhaustion or an end marker. A count without its value is consumed and retained
for the next call. With a zero budget, an active decoder performs a no-op:
consume nothing, emit nothing, and return `ended: false`.

Accepting a complete pair reserves its entire expanded count against the
constructor's cumulative byte cap, including output deferred to later calls.
Reject a pair that would exceed that cap with `LimitExceeded` before emitting
any byte of that pair. The cap is inclusive and does not reset per call.
A count alone does not trigger a cap error; a missing value is still truncation.
The zero count end marker consumes one byte and reserves no output.

On seeing an end marker, if any bytes remain in the same input, fail with
`TrailingData`; otherwise return `ended: true`. After a successful end marker,
empty pushes succeed with zero consumption/output and `ended: true`, including
with a zero budget. A nonempty push fails with `TrailingData`, even with a zero
budget. `finish` succeeds only after the end marker was consumed; repeated
successful `finish` calls succeed. Otherwise `finish` returns `Truncated`.
In particular, callers must drain pending output and resubmit the remaining
wire bytes before `finish`; it does not generate output or imply an end marker.

The first decoder error is terminal. Every subsequent `push` or `finish`
returns `Failed`, which takes precedence over all other conditions. On the
call returning the first error, any earlier output from that same call is
discarded (the API returns no batch); previous successful batches stay valid.
No error carries payload bytes or diagnostic text.

## Resource and completion requirements

Neither codec may accumulate the whole stream. Retained state must use memory
bounded independently of total input/output length, apart from the output
vector returned by the current call. Output allocation should follow actual
produced output, not blindly allocate `output_limit` bytes: `usize::MAX` is a
valid budget for a tiny stream. Decoder calls return at most their output
budget and do work proportional to input consumed plus output produced, with
constant overhead. Arithmetic must remain correct for `usize::MAX` limits.
Do not expose payload data through errors or external effects. Internal design
and additional nonbreaking conveniences are open.

# CSV column projection

Implement `csv_pick`, a small CLI for rearranging columns in CSV exports. Run it
as `csv_pick COLUMN [COLUMN ...]`: arguments are literal header names, in desired
output order. There are no options. A name beginning with `-` is still a name.
At least one argument is required and each must be a nonempty Unicode string.
Repeated selections are allowed and produce repeated output columns.

Read the entire CSV document from stdin and write the projected CSV to stdout.
The first record is the header. Header names must be nonempty and unique under
exact, case-sensitive comparison; do not trim whitespace, normalize Unicode,
or strip a BOM. Every selected name must exist. Every subsequent record must
have exactly the header's field count, including columns that are not selected.
Preserve record order and every selected field's decoded text exactly. Emit
the selected header followed by all projected data records. An input with just
a header succeeds.

The input dialect is precise:

- Input must be UTF-8. Comma separates fields; LF or CRLF separates records.
  The last record need not have a terminator. A final terminator adds no record.
- A blank line is a record containing one empty field, not a skipped line.
  A trailing comma adds an empty field. An entirely empty document has no header.
- A quoted field starts with `"` as its very first character. Within it, `""`
  represents one literal quote; commas, CR, LF, and CRLF are literal field text.
  After its closing quote only comma, record terminator, or EOF is permitted.
- In unquoted fields, a quote is invalid. A bare CR outside quotes is invalid.
  Spaces are ordinary field text, including spaces adjacent to quotes.
- No comment syntax or type conversion exists. All other Unicode characters
  are ordinary text.

Output must be valid CSV in this same dialect and preserve logical field values;
original quoting choices and record-terminator spelling need not be preserved.
You may use LF or CRLF output record terminators, with or without a final one.
Embedded CR and LF within field text must remain exact. Quoting every field is
permitted.

Successful execution exits 0 and leaves stderr empty. Invalid input must not
panic and must leave stdout empty. Emit a diagnostic on stderr containing the
applicable stable category token below, and no other category token. Exact prose
is unrestricted. Never echo argument values, header names, or field contents in
diagnostics; numeric positions and fixed explanatory text are permitted.

For overlapping failures, use this precedence over the whole document:

1. `E_USAGE`, exit 2: missing arguments, empty arguments, or non-Unicode arguments.
2. `E_INPUT`, exit 1: stdin read failure or invalid UTF-8.
3. `E_CSV`, exit 1: malformed CSV anywhere in the document.
4. `E_HEADER`, exit 1: absent/invalid header or any unknown selected name.
5. `E_WIDTH`, exit 1: any data record with the wrong field count.

Write/flush failure on stdout must exit 1 with `E_OUTPUT`; bytes already written
cannot be rolled back. Do not create or modify files, use the network, or launch
other processes. Ordinary memory buffering is allowed: assessed inputs are at
most 1 MiB and do not require a size-limit feature. Allocation failure is outside
scope. Choose your own functions, representation, and dependencies. The package
and binary name remain `csv_pick`. Add adequate own behavioral tests; hidden
checks are separate. Use the supplied `./cargo` launcher for every Cargo command.

# Subscription delivery with independent lifetimes

Implement the `subscription_mailbox` library in this starter. A broker distributes
owned text messages to subscriptions. This is an in-process library; no network,
filesystem access, timers, external services, or background runtime setup is needed.

Keep this public API:

```rust
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub struct Closed;

#[derive(Clone)]
pub struct Broker { /* implementation chosen by you */ }
pub struct Subscription { /* implementation chosen by you */ }

impl Broker {
    pub fn new() -> Self;
    pub fn subscribe(&self) -> Result<Subscription, Closed>;
    pub fn publish(&self, message: String) -> Result<usize, Closed>;
    pub fn close(&self);
}
impl Subscription {
    pub async fn recv(&mut self) -> Option<String>;
}
```

`Broker` must be `Send + Sync + Clone`; `Subscription` and its receive future
must be `Send`. Additional public conveniences are allowed but unnecessary.

Behavior:

- A new broker is open. Clones share the same subscriptions and close state.
- A subscription sees every publication after it subscribes, once, in FIFO order.
  It sees no earlier publication. Subscriptions receive independently: a slow
  subscriber cannot consume another subscriber's copy or delay publication.
  There is no message capacity or loss policy in this task. Empty strings,
  Unicode, and embedded NUL bytes are ordinary payloads and are preserved exactly.
- `publish` completes synchronously, without waiting for receivers to run, and
  returns the number of live subscriptions to which it delivered the message.
  With no subscribers it returns `Ok(0)`. Dropping a subscription detaches it;
  after that drop completes it is excluded from later delivery counts.
- `recv` waits when open and empty. A pending receive must make progress when
  a message arrives or the broker closes; it must not busy-wait. Dropping a
  receive future before it returns `Ready` never consumes or loses a message
  and never detaches the subscription, including if a message becomes available
  while that future is pending. The next receive can obtain that message.
- `close` is synchronous, global across clones, and idempotent. After it returns,
  publication and subscription creation both return `Err(Closed)`. Closure wins
  even when there are no subscribers or the payload is empty. Existing
  subscriptions drain all already delivered messages, then return `None` on
  every subsequent receive.
- Dropping any one broker clone does not close the broker while another remains.
  Dropping the final broker has the same drain-and-terminate effect as `close`.
  A subscription must not keep a publisher alive. Dropping one subscription
  never closes other subscriptions.
- Concurrent broker operations are linearizable: each behaves as if it happened
  at one point between invocation and return. All subscriptions present for the
  same concurrent publications observe the same order. A racing drop or close
  may fall on either side of a publication; it must not produce a partial
  publication to subscriptions that remain live throughout.

Ordinary valid calls must not panic. No diagnostics or payload logging is
required; do not write payloads to external output. Allocation failure is outside
scope. Choose storage, synchronization, and any supported library mechanisms;
Tokio is available in the starter, but its use is not prescribed. Construction,
publication, and closure must also work outside an entered Tokio runtime.

Add adequate own tests for the public behavior. Run the project-local `./cargo`
launcher for Cargo commands. Keep Cargo.lock consistent and validate with locked
dependency resolution. Deliver an implemented library and passing own tests.

Resolved direct dependency: Tokio 1.54.1 with sync. A registered receiver waker may run synchronously within UnboundedSender::send; dropping the last sender may also wake it. These are supplied dependency facts, not observed execution of this program. A subscription Drop can temporarily upgrade its Weak reference while another thread drops the final Broker. Custom wakers may call public broker operations; the contract does not prohibit reentry. Evaluate these facts only when deciding whether a proposed clarity change preserves its ownership and ordering obligations.
